title: Building a Multi-Page Looker Studio Dashboard on Validated GA4 BigQuery Views
goal: Build a multi-page, interactive Looker Studio dashboard on top of Session 1's validated BigQuery views -- adding device-grain and daily-grain sources -- that turns the three locked channel findings (volume != quality, Paid Search conversion lag, and the view_item -> add_to_cart funnel leak) into an executive-ready BI product, with every visual reconciled to a backing SQL query.
context:
I chose Session 2 to continue the natural arc of an analytics project: Session 1 produced validated SQL and three locked findings; the obvious next job for an analyst is to turn those findings into an interactive BI product a stakeholder can actually read and explore. Session 2 therefore builds directly on Session 1's artifact — the validated BigQuery view vw_channel_funnel — and layers a multi-page Looker Studio dashboard on top of it, adding two finer-grain data sources (a daily-trend view and a device-segment view) so the dashboard can support trend and segmentation narratives, not just a single channel cut.
What makes it different from Session 1. Session 1 was code-based: every step was SQL that produced an executable, numeric output I could diff and validate cold. Session 2 is GUI-based: Looker Studio is drag-and-configure, and most steps produce a chart, not a query result. The complexity moves from query logic to (a) modeling three data sources so they stay mutually consistent, (b) building calculated fields and cross-page interactivity, and (c) keeping every visual reconciled to a single source of truth. To preserve Session 1's validation discipline in a tool with no diff-able output, each dashboard component carries a backing SQL query that reproduces the numbers the chart should show — that is the GUI-era equivalent of "every step emits verifiable numbers."
Is it more difficult than Session 1? More complex in surface area (three sources instead of one, calculated fields, multi-page navigation, cross-filtering), and harder to validate because there is no automatic diff — I have to reconcile each visual against a backing query by eye. The raw SQL itself is lighter than Session 1's. Net: comparable-to-harder, with the difficulty concentrated in modeling consistency and validation rather than in writing queries.
Does "forcing" AI use affect the goal choice? For the SQL parts, using Claude is already my natural workflow, so the requirement changes nothing. For the Looker Studio GUI parts, a few steps are things I'd normally just click through myself; there, the seven-touchpoint rule feels slightly more deliberate than my natural flow, though prompting Claude for build specs and backing queries did add real structure.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: The dashboard was built end to end on Session 1's validated foundation. The two finer-grain views (vw_daily_channel_trend, vw_device_channel_funnel) reconcile to vw_channel_funnel by construction — both derive from vw_session_enriched and inherit channel from the shared, deterministic first-touch vw_user_channel — and the executive KPIs tie exactly to Session 1: 360,129 sessions, 4,848 purchases, $362,165 revenue, and AOV $74.70. The three locked findings are represented across the channel, funnel-leak, and trend pages, each with a backing SQL query.

Step 1.step_name: Build the two finer-grain BigQuery views (data foundation)
Step 1.step_action: Prompt Claude to scaffold two new views: vw_daily_channel_trend (adds an event_dt grain) and vw_device_channel_funnel (adds a device_category grain), each reusing vw_channel_funnel's exact channel CASE and stage-metric definitions verbatim. Run the V1-V3 validation queries and confirm each view reconciles back to the parent view before proceeding.
Step 1.input: vw_channel_funnel definition — channel CASE (keyed on medium), stage/metric expressions, revenue field, and _TABLE_SUFFIX date window.
Step 1.output: Two views that compile and reconcile to the parent — reconciliation query returns purch_diff = 0 and rev_diff = 0 per channel; no Unassigned row (or ≈ 0); daily view has full date coverage with no NULL event_dt; device view has exactly {desktop, mobile, tablet}, no NULLs.
rubrics: Both views compile and run against the public GA4 dataset without error
Each view reconciles exactly to vw_channel_funnel (purch_diff = rev_diff = 0)
Channel classification is keyed on medium only (no source‑substring matching); obfuscation tokens <Other> / (data deleted) carry explicit labeled buckets so Unassigned ≈ 0
Grain sanity passes (date coverage complete; device categories exactly the expected three, no NULLs).

ratings.output_quality_reason: Both child views derive from vw_session_enriched and inherit channel from the shared, deterministic vw_user_channel (first-touch via ARRAY_AGG(medium ORDER BY event_timestamp … LIMIT 1)), so per-channel roll-up to vw_channel_funnel is a construction identity, not a coincidence. The reconciliation query correctly diffs sessions/purchases/revenue per channel and returned 0/0 per the run. Channel is classified on medium only (no source substrings); both obfuscation tokens carry labeled buckets and Unassigned is the fallback (≈0). The deployed daily view is named vw_daily_channel_trend, matching the plan. This also implements the deterministic first-touch fix that replaced Session 1's non-deterministic ANY_VALUE(medium).

goal_achievement.Why or why not: produced both CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW statements and a correct reconciliation query, reusing the shared channel/stage logic verbatim.

Step 2.step_name: Connect and model the three sources in Looker Studio
Step 2.step_action: Add the three BigQuery views (vw_channel_funnel, vw_daily_channel_trend, vw_device_channel_funnel) as Looker Studio data sources. Set field types, default aggregations, and semantic types (date, currency), rename fields for readability, and create the source-level calculated fields the pages depend on (stage-to-stage conversion rates, AOV).
Step 2.input: The three validated views from Step 1; backing SQL for each calculated field.
Step 2.output: Three connected sources with correct types/aggregations; calculated fields whose values match their backing SQL.
rubrics: All three sources connect and every field has the correct type, aggregation, and semantic type
Each calculated field reproduces its backing‑SQL value (spot‑checked at ≥1 known row)
No aggregation traps (e.g., averaging a pre‑aggregated rate) — rates recomputed from summed numerators/denominators
Field naming is consistent and stakeholder‑readable across all three sources.

ratings.output_quality_reason: All three sources connected to Looker Studio successfully. Field types are checked and corrected. Relevant calculated fields are identified during the setup. All fields are backed by a SQL-query.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: the calculated-field formulas and backing SQL were correct; the semantic-type and naming polish weren't fully carried into the applied Looker source.

Step 3.step_name: Executive page - KPI scorecards + overall funnel
Step 3.step_action: Build the landing page: scorecards for headline KPIs (sessions/users, purchases, revenue, overall conversion rate, AOV) plus an overall funnel visual (view_item -> add_to_cart -> begin_checkout -> purchase) sourced from vw_channel_funnel. Prompt Claude for the build spec (chart type, source, dimensions, metrics, filters) and a backing query per scorecard.
Step 3.output: Executive page where every scorecard matches its backing query and the funnel totals tie to the parent view.
rubrics: Every scorecard value equals its backing‑SQL value
Funnel stage totals reconcile to vw_channel_funnel
KPI definitions (conversion rate, AOV) are stated and consistent with Session 1's formulas
Page reads as an executive summary — headline numbers legible without drill‑down.

ratings.output_quality_reason: Scorecards verified against Session 1: Session Count 360,129 and Reached Purchase 4,848 are the exact funnel total and endpoint; Session Revenue $362,165 and AOV $74.70 reconcile (362,165 / 4,848 = 74.70). The page reads as an executive summary. The one gap (rubric 3): the conversion KPI is viewItem_purchase_rate = 6.29% (purchases / view_items), a different denominator than Session 1's session-based conversion (~1.35%). The label is honest about which it is, but a stakeholder comparing to Session 1 will see 6.29% vs 1.35% without knowing they are different metrics — relabel it as a funnel-stage rate or add the session-based rate to match Session 1.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: scorecard specs and backing queries were produced and the values reconcile; the conversion-basis choice is yours to reconcile against Session 1.

Step 4.step_name: Channel performance page - volume vs. conversion + AOV
Step 4.step_action: Build the channel page visualizing the volume-vs-quality disparity (finding 1) and Paid Search conversion lag (finding 2): a volume-vs-conversion comparison (e.g., dual-axis or scatter), an AOV-by-channel bar, and a conversion-index calculated field (each channel's conversion rate indexed to the all-channel average) to make the lag read at a glance.
Step 4.input: vw_channel_funnel; backing SQL for the conversion index.
Step 4.output: Channel page where the volume/conversion and AOV visuals and the conversion index match their backing queries; Paid Search visibly reads below the 100 index line.
rubrics: Visuals correctly surface findings 1 and 2 (high‑volume/low‑quality channels and Paid Search lag are visually obvious)
The conversion‑index field matches its backing SQL and is centered correctly on the all‑channel average (= 100)
AOV values reconcile to the parent view per channel
Chart choices are honest (no dual‑axis distortion that overstates the gap).

ratings.output_quality_reason: The three backing queries are correct — the conversion index is centered on 100 from summed numerators/denominators, AOV = revenue/purchases, and both exclude the two obfuscation buckets. But the rendered channel visuals diverge from those queries: (1) the "viewItem_purchase_rate by channel" chart still includes both Unclassified buckets, and one is the tallest bar (~12%), so it does not match the 4-row backing query and lets a non-actionable bucket read as the best converter — the opposite of finding 1/2; (2) the "purchase_revenue_rate by channel" chart is AOV mis-scaled to ~7,500% (the Step-2 semantic-type slip). The fix is a chart/page-level channel filter plus a currency format; the SQL itself is sound. Scored on the rendered state, per the reconciliation discipline..

goal_achievement.Why or why not: correct backing SQL and the right exclusion logic were provided; the exclusion filter and currency format were not applied to the rendered Looker charts.

Step 5.step_name: Funnel-leak page - stage drop-off + device split
Step 5.step_action: Build the funnel-leak page highlighting the view_item -> add_to_cart drop (finding 3): a stage-to-stage drop-off visual with the leak stage emphasized, plus a device split of that same leak using vw_device_channel_funnel to show whether the leak concentrates on a device. Prompt Claude for the build spec and a backing query for the leak rate overall and per device.
Step 5.input: vw_channel_funnel, vw_device_channel_funnel; backing SQL for leak rate.
Step 5.output: Funnel-leak page where the overall leak rate matches its backing query and the device split sums back to the overall figure.
rubrics: The view_item → add_to_cart leak is the visually dominant element and its rate matches backing SQL
The device split reconciles to the overall leak (sums across device tie out)
Stage ordering and drop‑off math are correct (no double‑counting across stages)
The page answers "where does the leak concentrate?" without extra clicks.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The funnel-leak page is built successfully. Backing query complements the build.

Step 6.step_name: Trend page - time series + date-range and channel controls
Step 6.step_action: Build the trend page from vw_daily_channel_trend: a conversion-rate and revenue time series over the dataset window, with a date-range control and a channel filter so the trend can be sliced by channel. Prompt Claude for the build spec and a backing query at one fixed date range to validate the series.
Step 6.input: vw_daily_channel_trend; backing SQL at a fixed date range.
Step 6.output: Trend page where the series at the fixed range matches its backing query and the channel filter partitions the series correctly.
rubrics: The time series at a fixed date range matches its backing query
The date‑range control and channel filter behave correctly (filtered totals still reconcile)
Date handling is correct (no gaps, no timezone/parse artifacts in event_dt)
Trend is legible and the axis scaling doesn't distort the movement.

ratings.output_quality_reason: Time series charts are produced successfully. The date range control and channel filter were applied.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: time series charts are produced as intended.

Step 7.step_name: Interactivity & polish - cross-page controls, cross-filtering, annotations, theme
Step 7.step_action: Finish the dashboard: add dashboard-wide controls, enable cross-filtering so clicking a channel/device filters related visuals, add short narrative annotations tying each page to its finding, and apply a consistent theme. Prompt Claude for an interactivity plan and a final consistency-check checklist.
Step 7.output: A coherent multi-page dashboard where cross-filtering works, annotations state each finding, theme is consistent, and a final pass confirms every page still reconciles to its backing queries.
rubrics: Cross‑filtering works across pages without breaking reconciliation
Each page carries a one‑line annotation naming its finding
Theme, fonts, and number formats are consistent across all pages
Final consistency check passes — no visual disagrees with its backing query.

ratings.output_quality_reason: Dashboard is finished. Checks are done. Rather than creating a distinct page for each step, I used one-page style during the session.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: dashboard finalized accordingly with the requirements I provided to the AI-agent.
